  "text": "The tailor’s shop had been empty for three years when Mara noticed a light in the window.

Inside, a woman was taking measurements of the walls.

“A bakery,” she explained through the open door. “If the wiring allows it.”

Mara nodded. Her mother had brought her here for school uniforms, standing behind her while the tailor pinned the hems.

“Did you know him?” the woman asked.

“A little.”

“There’s something you might want to see.”

Behind the counter, narrow pencil marks climbed the doorframe. Beside each was a name and date. The tailor had measured children there when their parents complained they were growing too quickly.

Mara found her name near the bottom.

Above it, four more marks recorded the years she had spent pretending not to enjoy the ritual.

The last was dated the summer before her mother died.

“We’re painting Monday,” the woman said, then stopped.

Mara ran a finger beside the marks, careful not to touch them.

“Could I photograph it?”

“Of course.”

She took several pictures, but the pencil barely showed on the screen.

On Sunday, the woman called. Mara had left her number without knowing why.

“My brother says the frame needs replacing anyway.”

When Mara arrived, the marked strip of wood lay on the counter, wrapped in a clean apron.

At home, she propped it against the kitchen wall.

Her son asked what it was.

“A record of me getting taller.”

He stood beside it, heels together.

Mara fetched a pencil. Then she rested a book on his head, just as the tailor had, and asked him to stand still."
